q: Carmen calls 'voy a' the one key that opens the whole future. What does 'Voy a' mean?
teach: From the lesson: the engine that every future sentence today is built on.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'Voy a… — I am going to… Voy comes from the verb ir — to go. I want you to feel that in your bones, because English does the exact same' Another way: voy comes from ir, to go — the same trick English uses in 'I am going to work.'
walk: Walk it through: (1) Carmen teaches one pattern for everyday future plans. (2) Its first-person form starts every 'I' future sentence in the lesson. (3) That form, voy a, means: I am going to.

walk: Walk it through: (1) The lesson dresses the wedding sentence with a time signpost. (2) Próximo means next and año means year. (3) So el próximo año means: next year.

q: Carmen talks about something Bill and Jillian will do together — getting married in Key West. Which form of the pattern does she use for 'we are going to'?
teach: From the lesson: the one small warning — the two engines, I and we.
teach2: From the lesson, in Carmen's words: 'voy a is for I — one man, alone, speaking about himself — and vamos a is for we — two or more, the team speaking about itself. Voy a' Another way: mine alone takes voy a; ours takes vamos a — nobody marries himself.
walk: Walk it through: (1) Carmen warns about mixing up the two engines. (2) Voy a is for I, one man speaking about himself. (3) The other engine is used when the subject is: we.
